pages.heading: 4.1 Bernoulli trials and the binomial count
paragraphs: Many experiments repeat one simple trial: flip a coin, take a shot, test a part. A Bernoulli trial has only two outcomes, which we call success and failure, with probabilities p and 1 − p. We speak of repeated trials when the trials are independent and every trial has the same success probability p.

Each trial comes with an indicator I that equals 1 on a success and 0 on a failure. Its mean is E[I] = 1·p + 0·(1 − p) = p, and since I² = I its variance is p − p² = p(1 − p). It is largest, 1/4, when p = 1/2.

Now let X count the successes in n repeated trials. A particular sequence with k successes and n − k failures has probability p^k (1 − p)^(n − k), because the trials are independent. Every such sequence has the same probability, and there are C(n, k) of them, one for each choice of which k positions hold the successes. Adding them up gives the binomial distribution: P(X = k) = C(n, k) p^k (1 − p)^(n − k) for k = 0, 1, …, n. We write X ~ Bin(n, p).
The binomial theorem shows that these probabilities add up to (p + (1 − p))^n = 1. The case n = 1 is a single Bernoulli trial.

pages.heading: 4.2 Mean, variance and waiting times
paragraphs: The mean of a binomial count has a short derivation. Write X = I_1 + ⋯ + I_n with one indicator per trial. Linearity of expectation, which needs no independence, gives E[X] = np. Because the trials are independent the variances also add, so Var(X) = np(1 − p). The standard deviation √(np(1 − p)) grows only like the square root of n.

Examples. Ten flips of a fair coin give exactly five heads with probability 252/1024, about 0.246: the most likely count, yet less likely than not. A player who scores 80% of free throws makes all of five shots with probability 0.8⁵ ≈ 0.328. If each of 20 parts is defective with probability 0.05, independently, none is defective with probability 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.358.

A different question is how long we wait for the first success. Let T be the number of trials up to and including it. The first success comes at trial k exactly when k − 1 failures are followed by a success, so P(T = k) = (1 − p)^(k − 1) p for k = 1, 2, … This is the geometric distribution, and its mean is 1/p. Rolling for a six takes six rolls on average. The geometric distribution is memoryless: having failed many times does not shorten the wait still ahead.

pages.heading: 4.3 Running averages and the law of large numbers
paragraphs: Watch a long run of trials and keep track of the proportion of successes so far, X/n. This running proportion is an average of indicators, so its mean is p and its variance is p(1 − p)/n. The spread of the proportion therefore shrinks like 1/√n: four times as many trials halve it.

The law of large numbers turns this into a statement about probabilities. For every tolerance ε > 0, the chance that the proportion is off from p by ε or more goes to zero: P(|X/n − p| ≥ ε) → 0 as n grows. In words, the running proportion settles near p. This is what makes the long-run frequency interpretation of probability consistent with the rules we have been using.

The law says nothing of the kind about the count itself. The difference X − np between the number of successes and its expected value typically grows like √n. After 100 fair flips it is usually within about 5 heads of 50; after a million flips a gap of several hundred heads is ordinary. The gap grows, but more slowly than n, so divided by n it disappears.
A plot of the running proportion shows this clearly: wild swings in the first few dozen trials, then a curve that stays inside an ever narrower band around p.

pages.heading: 4.4 Streaks and the gambler's misconception
paragraphs: After a fair coin lands heads five times in a row, many people feel that tails is now due. It is not. Independent trials have no memory, so the chance of heads on the next flip is still 1/2, whatever happened before.

How, then, does the proportion of heads come back to 1/2? Not by correction but by dilution. Suppose the first 10 flips were all heads. From then on we expect half of the remaining flips to be heads, so after n flips the expected number of heads is 10 + (n − 10)/2. The expected excess over n/2 stays at 5 heads forever: nothing pays it back. Yet the expected proportion is 1/2 + 5/n, which is 0.55 after 100 flips, 0.505 after 1000 and 0.5005 after 10 000. The streak is swamped by the flips that follow, not cancelled by them.

The same reasoning applies to roulette wheels, lottery numbers that have not come up in a while and a shooter who has missed several in a row: if the trials are truly independent with a fixed p, past results carry no information about the next one. When people do see real hot or cold streaks, the right conclusion is that the trials may not be independent, or that p may be changing, not that the future must balance the past.
